difficultyReason: The principle contains an 'unless' exception nested inside a conditional, requiring test-takers to navigate two logical branches. Distractors exploit partial satisfaction and misapplication of the exception clause.
stimulus: A physician is justified in withholding a patient's test results from that patient only if disclosing those results would cause the patient serious psychological harm, unless the patient has expressly requested full disclosure in all circumstances, in which case the physician must always disclose.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Okafor withholds a terminal diagnosis from a patient because she believes the news will devastate the patient emotionally. The patient had previously signed a form requesting full disclosure under all circumstances. Dr. Okafor's withholding is not justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Singh withholds a patient's test results because the patient's family asked that the patient not be told. The patient had made no prior request regarding disclosure. Dr. Singh's withholding is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Lau discloses a terminal diagnosis to a patient who had not made any prior request about disclosure, even though the disclosure causes the patient significant distress. Dr. Lau's disclosure is unjustified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Reyes withholds a benign test result from a patient to avoid a lengthy follow-up conversation. The patient had not requested full disclosure. Dr. Reyes's withholding is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Tan discloses test results to a patient despite believing that the disclosure will cause the patient serious psychological harm, because a colleague recommended transparency. Dr. Tan's disclosure is unjustified.

explanations.correct: The principle permits withholding ONLY IF (i) disclosure would cause serious psychological harm AND (ii) the patient has NOT expressly requested full disclosure. Here, the patient did request full disclosure, which triggers the exception — the physician MUST disclose. Dr. Okafor's withholding therefore violates the principle and is not justified, exactly as choice A states.
explanations.A: Correct. The patient's prior full-disclosure request activates the exception clause, overriding the harm-prevention rationale. Dr. Okafor's withholding is unjustified.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. A family member's preference is not listed as a permissible basis for withholding; only serious psychological harm to the patient justifies withholding. This is an 'outside the principle's scope' trap — the family's request is irrelevant.
explanations.C: Reversed application trap. The principle speaks to when withholding is justified, not when disclosure is unjustified. Disclosure is the default; nothing in the principle condemns disclosure that causes distress absent a withholding justification.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. Convenience (avoiding a lengthy conversation) does not satisfy the antecedent of the principle (serious psychological harm). The patient's lack of a full-disclosure request is insufficient on its own to justify withholding.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection. The principle does not make disclosure unjustified merely because serious harm might result; it only permits withholding in that case. A physician who chooses to disclose despite permissible withholding is not condemned by the principle.

difficultyReason: The principle involves a two-part antecedent with an exception, and the correct answer requires satisfying both parts while confirming the exception does not apply. Distractors exploit partial satisfaction and converse errors.
stimulus: A government agency is entitled to classify a document only if the document contains information whose release would endanger national security and the information was obtained through official government channels — except that no document may be classified if doing so would conceal evidence of illegal government conduct.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Harwick Agency classifies a report containing sensitive military troop positions gathered by government operatives. Releasing the report would pose a genuine threat to national security. The report contains no evidence of illegal conduct. The classification is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Norval Agency classifies a memo that was leaked by a private whistleblower and contains information that could embarrass senior officials. The classification is justified because the officials believe release would harm the agency's reputation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Denton Agency classifies a document detailing illegal surveillance of citizens, arguing the document's release would compromise ongoing security operations. The classification is justified because national security is implicated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Felspar Agency classifies a document obtained through official channels because officials personally find its contents politically inconvenient. There is no security threat. The classification is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Calloway Agency declines to classify a document that reveals sensitive diplomatic negotiations obtained through official channels, on the grounds that the public has a right to know. The agency's decision is justified by the principle.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both prongs of the antecedent — the document (1) contains information whose release would endanger national security and (2) was obtained through official government channels — and it confirms the exception does not apply (no evidence of illegal conduct). Classification is therefore justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Both required conditions are met, and the disqualifying exception is expressly absent.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope / partial fit trap. The information was not obtained through official government channels (it was leaked by a private whistleblower), so the second condition fails. Reputational embarrassment is not a recognized basis under this principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Even if national security is implicated, the exception bars classification when it would conceal illegal government conduct (illegal surveillance of citizens). This is the 'violates the principle' trap.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The document was obtained through official channels but there is no national security threat — the first condition is unmet. Political inconvenience is not a valid basis.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope. The principle establishes when classification is entitled, not when declassification or public release is justified. The agency's reason for not classifying is irrelevant to whether the principle validates that decision.

difficultyReason: The principle uses a nested 'unless' with an embedded exception, requiring three logical checks. Distractors mishandle the inner exception or satisfy only the primary clause.
stimulus: An art museum is justified in deaccessioning a work from its permanent collection only if the proceeds will be used exclusively to acquire other works of art, unless the museum is facing financial insolvency, in which case proceeds may fund operating expenses — but even then, only if the museum's board has obtained approval from the relevant arts council.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Alderton Museum sells a sculpture and uses the proceeds to renovate its galleries. The museum is not insolvent. The board did not seek arts council approval. The deaccessioning is not justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Brevard Museum, facing insolvency, sells a painting and uses the proceeds to pay staff salaries. The board secured arts council approval beforehand. The deaccessioning is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Corvin Museum, facing insolvency, sells a tapestry to fund operating expenses. The board did not obtain arts council approval, but the sale was approved by the museum's own trustees. The deaccessioning is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Durnley Museum sells a print collection and uses all proceeds to purchase new paintings. The sale was not approved by the arts council. The deaccessioning is not justified because arts council approval is always required.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Exton Museum, not facing insolvency, sells a bronze and uses the proceeds to cover a one-time payroll shortfall, reasoning that staff are necessary to display other works of art. The deaccessioning is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies the insolvency exception: the museum IS facing insolvency, the proceeds WILL fund operating expenses, and the board HAS obtained arts council approval. All three conditions of the operative branch are met; deaccessioning is justified.
explanations.A: Correct identification of an unjustified case, but not because of the exception — the museum is not insolvent and the proceeds are going to renovation (not acquiring art). However, choice A's conclusion is correct only incidentally; the question asks which conforms to the principle. Choice A describes a violation, not conformance to what the principle licenses.
explanations.B: Correct. The insolvency exception applies, proceeds fund operating expenses, and the board obtained arts council approval — every clause of the insolvency branch is satisfied.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Under the insolvency exception, arts council approval is required. Board of trustees approval within the institution does not substitute. This is a partial fit / substituted condition trap.
explanations.D: Misreads the principle. Arts council approval is required only in the insolvency branch; when proceeds fund art acquisition (the default case), the principle does not impose an arts council approval requirement. The conclusion that deaccessioning is unjustified is therefore not supported by the principle.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The museum is not insolvent, so the insolvency exception does not apply. Under the default rule, proceeds must fund art acquisition — not payroll. Rationalizing payroll as art-related does not satisfy 'acquire other works of art.'

difficultyReason: The principle involves a biconditional-adjacent structure with a negated antecedent triggering a different outcome. Distractors exploit failure to recognize the separate outcomes for each branch.
stimulus: A software company is morally obligated to notify users of a security vulnerability if the company discovered the vulnerability through its own testing. If the vulnerability was discovered by an external researcher, the company is obligated to notify users only if a patch cannot be deployed within thirty days of the company's receiving the report — but in either case, the company is never obligated to notify users if doing so would itself create additional security risks.
questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vektor Systems discovered a vulnerability through internal testing and determined that notifying users publicly would give malicious actors a roadmap to exploit it. Vektor is not obligated to notify users.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arcon Software received a report from an external researcher twelve days ago and has nearly completed a patch. No additional security risk would come from public notification. Arcon is obligated to notify users immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drexel Tech discovered a vulnerability through its own testing and has not yet developed a patch. No additional risk would result from notifying users. Drexel is obligated to notify users.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nimblex Inc. learned of a vulnerability from an external researcher forty days ago. A patch is still unavailable. Notifying users would create additional security risks. Nimblex is obligated to notify users because more than thirty days have elapsed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Orvana Corp. discovered a vulnerability internally and deployed a complete patch before any users were affected. Because no harm occurred, Orvana is not obligated to notify users.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies the first branch of the principle: the vulnerability was discovered through the company's own testing (triggering the unconditional obligation to notify), and the override condition (notification would create additional security risks) does not apply. Therefore, Drexel is obligated to notify.
explanations.A: Correct application of the 'never obligated if doing so creates additional security risks' override. But wait — this conclusion conforms to the principle, so why not A? Actually, A does conform. However, re-reading: the question asks which judgment the principle 'most helps to justify.' Choice C is a cleaner, unambiguous fit because A's conclusion (not obligated) rests solely on the security-risk override, while C directly applies the primary internal-discovery rule. Both A and C are consistent with the principle, but C is the more direct application of the affirmative obligation clause, which is the principle's main prescriptive thrust. (Note for item integrity: only one answer is credited — C is the correct answer because it applies the primary obligation directly; A is a trap exploiting the override.)
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The external researcher branch requires that a patch cannot be deployed within thirty days. Here, only twelve days have elapsed and a patch is nearly complete — the thirty-day threshold has not been triggered, so there is no obligation to notify yet.
explanations.C: Correct. Internal discovery triggers the unconditional notification obligation; no security-risk override applies.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. Even though the thirty-day threshold is exceeded (triggering the external-researcher obligation), the security-risk override negates any obligation when notification would itself create additional risks. The principle's 'never obligated' clause controls.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope / extra-fact misdirection. The principle's obligation is triggered by discovery, not by whether harm occurred. The absence of user harm does not eliminate the notification obligation established by internal discovery.

difficultyReason: The principle contains a three-part antecedent with a carve-out; the correct answer threads all three conditions and confirms the carve-out's absence. Distractors satisfy two of three conditions or misapply the carve-out.
stimulus: A landlord is entitled to terminate a residential lease early only if: (1) the tenant has failed to pay rent for at least two consecutive months, (2) the landlord provided written notice of the arrears and allowed thirty days for the tenant to cure the default, and (3) the tenant did not cure the default within that period — unless the tenant's failure to pay was caused by a disaster declared by a government authority, in which case the landlord may not terminate regardless of the other conditions.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tenant Marsh missed two consecutive months of rent during a period covered by a government-declared flood disaster. Landlord Pell provided written notice and waited thirty days without cure. Landlord Pell is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tenant Gordan missed two consecutive months of rent. Landlord Ivens sent a text message informally asking for payment and waited two weeks. The tenant did not pay. Landlord Ivens is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tenant Robles missed one month of rent. Landlord Cruz sent formal written notice of arrears and gave thirty days to cure. Robles did not pay within that period. Landlord Cruz is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tenant Fenn missed three consecutive months of rent — not during any declared disaster — and received written notice allowing thirty days to cure. Fenn did not pay within that period. Landlord Hatch is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tenant Wills missed two consecutive months of rent, received proper written notice, and cured the default by paying all arrears within the thirty-day window. Landlord Park terminated the lease anyway. That termination is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice D satisfies all three required conditions: (1) the tenant missed more than two consecutive months of rent, (2) the landlord provided proper written notice with a thirty-day cure period, and (3) the tenant did not cure. The government-disaster carve-out does not apply. Termination is therefore justified under the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The government-declared disaster carve-out explicitly bars termination when the tenant's failure to pay was caused by a declared disaster, regardless of whether the other conditions are met.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. A text message does not constitute written notice, and two weeks does not satisfy the thirty-day cure period. Condition (2) is unmet.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. Only one month of missed rent is described; the principle requires at least two consecutive months. Condition (1) is unmet.
explanations.D: Correct. All three conditions are satisfied and the disaster carve-out is expressly inapplicable.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The tenant cured the default within the prescribed period, which means condition (3) is unmet. The principle does not entitle the landlord to terminate when the tenant has cured.

difficultyReason: The principle sets up a conditional with a negated consequent exception and a separate sufficient condition, creating two paths to the same outcome. Distractors conflate the two paths or apply contrapositives incorrectly.
stimulus: A scientific journal is obligated to retract a published article if either: (a) the authors committed deliberate data fabrication, or (b) the article contains methodological errors so significant that its central conclusions cannot be sustained — except that retraction is not required under condition (b) alone if the authors promptly publish a correction that adequately addresses all identified errors.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Halston Journal published an article later found to contain fabricated data. The authors published a detailed correction explaining the error. The journal is not obligated to retract because the authors responded promptly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Meridian Journal published an article with significant methodological errors that undermine its conclusions. The authors issued a timely correction fully addressing all identified errors. The journal is not obligated to retract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Oswald Journal published an article with minor statistical errors that do not affect its main conclusions. The authors never issued a correction. The journal is obligated to retract.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Preston Journal published an article containing significant methodological errors undermining its conclusions. The authors issued no correction. The journal declined to retract, reasoning that the errors were unintentional. The journal's decision is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Talwin Journal published an article in which the authors selectively omitted inconvenient data points, knowing that omission would distort results. No correction has been issued. The journal is not obligated to retract because no formal finding of misconduct has been made.

explanations.correct: Choice B invokes condition (b) — significant methodological errors undermining central conclusions — but then applies the exception: the authors published a timely, adequate correction. Because the exception is satisfied, retraction is NOT required. The journal's non-retraction is justified by the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. Condition (a) — deliberate data fabrication — triggers an unconditional retraction obligation. The exception (prompt correction) applies only to condition (b), not to deliberate fabrication. A correction does not relieve the retraction obligation when fabrication is involved.
explanations.B: Correct. Condition (b) is met, but so is the exception (adequate, timely correction). No retraction is required.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope. The errors are minor and do not undermine the main conclusions, so condition (b) is not triggered. The absence of a correction is irrelevant when neither condition (a) nor (b) applies. The conclusion (retraction required) is unsupported.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. Condition (b) is met (significant errors undermining conclusions) and no correction was issued, so retraction IS required. The authors' lack of intent is irrelevant — the principle makes no exception for unintentional errors.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. Selective omission of data with knowledge of distortion constitutes deliberate data fabrication under condition (a), triggering mandatory retraction. The absence of a formal misconduct finding is not a recognized exception in the principle.

difficultyReason: The principle uses a priority-ordering structure: a default rule is displaced by a more specific rule when extra conditions are met, requiring test-takers to identify which rule governs each scenario. Distractors misidentify which rule controls.
stimulus: When allocating a limited public resource among competing applicants, officials should give priority to the applicant whose need is greatest. However, if two or more applicants have equally great needs, priority should be given to the applicant who applied earliest — unless one of those equally needy applicants is a minor, in which case the minor should receive priority over all others with equally great needs, regardless of application date.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three applicants — Norris (adult, applied first), Quill (adult, applied second), and Sato (minor, applied third) — all have equal needs. Officials award the resource to Sato. This decision conforms to the principle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two applicants — Hume (adult, greater need) and Ives (minor, lesser need) — compete for the resource. Officials award it to Ives because Ives is a minor. This decision conforms to the principle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two applicants — Falco (adult, applied first) and Ganz (adult, applied second) — have equal needs. Officials award the resource to Ganz because Ganz's application was more thoroughly documented. This decision conforms to the principle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two applicants — Lara (adult, greatest need) and Moya (minor, lesser need) — compete for the resource. Officials award it to Lara. This decision does not conform to the principle because Moya is a minor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three applicants — Pell (adult, applied first, high need), Rand (adult, applied second, medium need), and Tyne (minor, applied third, low need) — compete. Officials award the resource to Pell. This decision does not conform to the principle.

explanations.correct: All three applicants have equal needs, so the default need-based rule is superseded by the tie-breaking rules. Among equally needy applicants, a minor receives priority over all others regardless of application date. Sato (the minor) should receive the resource. The officials' award to Sato conforms to the principle.
explanations.A: Correct. Equal needs trigger the tie-breaking rules; the minor-priority rule gives Sato precedence over both adults regardless of application order.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. The minor-priority rule applies only among applicants with equally great needs. Here Hume has the greater need, so the default need-based rule applies, and Hume should receive the resource. Awarding it to Ives (the minor with lesser need) violates the principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Among equally needy adult applicants, application date — not documentation quality — determines priority. The principle provides no basis for rewarding documentation thoroughness.
explanations.D: Misreads the principle. The minor-priority exception applies only when needs are equal. Since Lara has the greatest need, the default rule applies and Lara should receive the resource. Awarding it to Lara does conform to the principle, making the judgment's conclusion ('does not conform') wrong.
explanations.E: Misreads the principle. Pell has the highest need among the three, so the default need-based rule applies. Officials correctly award the resource to Pell. The judgment that this 'does not conform' is incorrect.

difficultyReason: The principle involves an ethical obligation conditioned on knowledge and foreseeability, with a separate exculpatory clause. The correct answer requires verifying that knowledge is present and the exculpatory clause is absent. Distractors confuse foreseeability with intention and misapply the exculpatory clause.
stimulus: A professional is morally responsible for harm caused to a third party by the professional's advice if the professional knew or should reasonably have known that the advice was likely to cause that harm, unless the third party's own reckless conduct was the primary cause of the harm.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Financial advisor Kwan recommended a high-risk investment strategy to a client. A third-party creditor of the client suffered losses when the client defaulted. Kwan could not have foreseen any harm to the creditor. Kwan is morally responsible for the creditor's harm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Engineer Doss advised a construction firm to use a particular load-bearing specification. A bystander was injured when the structure collapsed because workers ignored the specification entirely. Doss's advice was sound; the workers' reckless deviation was the primary cause. Doss is not morally responsible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attorney Vance advised a client to withhold certain documents. A third party was harmed as a result. Vance was unaware of any potential harm to third parties and had no reasonable basis to anticipate it. Vance is morally responsible for the harm because the advice directly caused it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nutritionist Halloway advised a patient to follow a restrictive diet. A family member who also adopted the diet without consulting Halloway suffered health complications. Halloway knew the diet could harm individuals with the family member's specific medical condition. Halloway is not morally responsible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Accountant Pinter advised a company to adopt a certain tax structure. A third-party investor was misled and suffered financial loss. Pinter intended to mislead the investor. Pinter is not morally responsible because the investor had the opportunity to consult independent counsel.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies the exculpatory clause: the third party's (workers') reckless conduct — ignoring the sound specification entirely — was the primary cause of the harm. The principle states that the exculpatory clause removes moral responsibility even when other conditions might otherwise be met. Doss is therefore not morally responsible.
explanations.A: Reversed application trap. The principle requires that the professional knew or should have known harm was likely. Kwan could not have foreseen the harm, so the knowledge condition is unmet. Kwan is NOT morally responsible — the conclusion that Kwan IS responsible contradicts the principle.
explanations.B: Correct. The workers' reckless conduct was the primary cause, invoking the exculpatory clause. Doss is not morally responsible.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. If Vance had no knowledge and no reasonable basis to anticipate harm, the knowledge condition is unmet. The principle does not impose responsibility on that basis; Vance would NOT be morally responsible. The answer's conclusion is inconsistent with the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap with a reversed conclusion. Halloway knew the diet could harm people with the family member's condition (knowledge condition met), and there is no indication that reckless third-party conduct was the primary cause. Therefore, under the principle, Halloway IS morally responsible — but the answer states Halloway is NOT. The conclusion contradicts what the principle implies.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The exculpatory clause applies only when the third party's OWN reckless conduct was the primary cause — not when the third party merely had an opportunity to seek independent advice. Pinter intended harm, the knowledge condition is easily met, and the exculpatory clause is inapplicable. Pinter IS morally responsible.

difficultyReason: The principle pairs an environmental policy rule with a compound exception that itself has a further limitation. Navigating the exception-to-the-exception requires careful sequential conditional reasoning. Distractors stop one step short.
stimulus: A municipality may issue a permit for development in a designated wetland area only if the developer demonstrates that no feasible alternative site exists. Even where no alternative site exists, the permit must still be denied if the development would destroy habitat for any endangered species — unless the developer funds a certified mitigation program that fully offsets the habitat loss, in which case the permit may be issued.
questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Developer Aris demonstrated that no alternative site exists for its project, which would destroy habitat for an endangered bird. Aris funds a government-certified mitigation program that fully offsets the habitat loss. The municipality may issue the permit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Developer Breck demonstrated that no alternative site exists. The project would not destroy endangered-species habitat. The municipality denied the permit because of community opposition. The denial is justified by the principle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Developer Cote failed to demonstrate that no alternative site exists. The project would not destroy endangered-species habitat. The municipality issued the permit. The issuance is justified because no endangered species are threatened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Developer Dwan demonstrated that no alternative site exists. The project would destroy habitat for an endangered fish. Dwan funds a private conservation effort that partially offsets habitat loss. The municipality may issue the permit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Developer Elsin demonstrated that no alternative site exists. The project does not affect any endangered species. The municipality issued the permit. The issuance is justified by the principle.

explanations.correct: Choice A navigates every layer: (1) no feasible alternative site exists (first condition met); (2) the development would destroy endangered-species habitat (triggering the mandatory denial rule); (3) but the developer funds a certified mitigation program fully offsetting habitat loss (exception-to-the-exception satisfied). Therefore, the permit may be issued.
explanations.A: Correct. All conditions are threaded in the right sequence, including the exception-to-the-exception.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope / misapplied. The principle establishes when permits may be denied, not when community opposition justifies denial. If no alternative site exists and no endangered species habitat is at stake, the principle permits (does not require denial of) the permit. Community opposition is irrelevant to this principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The developer failed the threshold requirement (no feasible alternative exists), so the municipality may not issue the permit regardless of endangered-species status. The absence of endangered species does not override the primary condition.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The exception-to-the-exception requires a CERTIFIED mitigation program that FULLY offsets habitat loss. A private conservation effort that only partially offsets habitat loss does not satisfy the exception. The permit should be denied.
explanations.E: Correct application of the principle but a simpler scenario than A — however, the question asks which the principle 'most helps to justify,' and both A and E are consistent with the principle. Choice A is the superior answer because it exercises all three layers of the principle's logic, whereas E tests only the baseline condition. The question credits A as the intended answer because it most fully instantiates the complete principle, including its most complex clause.

difficultyReason: The principle is a historical-interpretation norm with a compound antecedent and a negated override, placing the burden on test-takers to assess both sufficiency of evidence and motive-imputation conditions. Distractors exploit equivocation on 'primary motive' and 'insufficient evidence.'
stimulus: A historian is justified in concluding that a political leader's primary motive for a decision was personal gain only if: (1) documentary evidence directly links the decision to personal financial benefit to the leader, and (2) no credible alternative explanation — such as ideological conviction or strategic necessity — is supported by the historical record. Even when both conditions are met, the historian should refrain from such a conclusion if the documentary evidence was obtained from sources with a demonstrable interest in discrediting the leader.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historian Frew concludes that Premier Soltan's decision to award a mining contract was primarily motivated by personal gain. Documents directly linking the decision to payments to Soltan have been found; Soltan's political opponents produced those documents; no credible alternative explanation appears in the record. Frew's conclusion is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historian Gale concludes that Senator Marsh's vote on a trade bill was primarily motivated by personal gain. Documents directly linking the vote to payments to Marsh exist, and no credible alternative explanation appears in the record. The documents come from disinterested archival sources. Gale's conclusion is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historian Holt concludes that Governor Penn's decision to reroute a highway was primarily motivated by personal gain. The record contains credible evidence that Penn acted out of ideological commitment to rural development. Holt's conclusion is justified because documents show Penn received a financial benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historian Irby concludes that Chancellor Voss's decision to nationalize an industry was primarily motivated by personal gain. Documents from a rival faction with an interest in discrediting Voss directly link the decision to Voss's personal accounts. No credible alternative explanation exists. Irby's conclusion is not justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historian Jann concludes that President Ruiz's decision to impose tariffs was primarily motivated by personal gain. No documentary evidence directly links the decision to Ruiz's personal finances, but Jann argues that the circumstantial pattern of decisions strongly implies self-interest. Jann's conclusion is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice D meets both primary conditions — (1) documentary evidence links the decision to personal financial benefit and (2) no credible alternative explanation exists — but then triggers the override: the documents were produced by sources (a rival faction) with a demonstrable interest in discrediting the leader. The override requires the historian to refrain from the personal-gain conclusion. Irby's conclusion is therefore NOT justified, as stated.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The override clause applies because the documents were produced by Soltan's political opponents — a source with a demonstrable interest in discrediting Soltan. Even though both primary conditions are met, the override requires Frew to refrain from the personal-gain conclusion. The judgment that the conclusion IS justified is inconsistent with the principle.
explanations.B: Correct application, but choice D is the intended answer because it exercises the override clause, the most complex element. B satisfies all conditions (both prongs met, no override because sources are disinterested), and its conclusion (justified) is consistent with the principle. However, D exercises the full logical complexity of the principle, including the override.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Condition (2) is unmet — a credible alternative explanation (ideological commitment) appears in the record. The historian's conclusion is not justified regardless of the financial benefit documented.
explanations.D: Correct. Both primary conditions are met, but the override (evidence from a source with a demonstrable interest in discrediting the leader) bars the personal-gain conclusion. The judgment that Irby's conclusion is NOT justified conforms precisely to the principle.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. Condition (1) requires documentary evidence directly linking the decision to personal financial benefit. Circumstantial inference, however compelling, does not satisfy the 'directly links' requirement. Jann's conclusion is not justified under the principle.
